items.title: David Finck interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, May 29, 2015
items.q: I can’t tell you how many times I’ve heard a James Brown drum part, or even James Brown making a sound inserted into somebody’s song.

ctx.x: Yeah. You know it is interesting when you’re doing a record for a singer, I’ve done some studio work, and if no one is singing, especially from a piano player, like you’re thinking maybe I shouldn’t be playing here. What am I covering up potentially. And that’s a weird feeling.

It is a weird feeling. Along with what you experienced, it affects the overall flow of a song. I happen to know a lot of songs, I love songs and songwriters and so often times I know the tune and kind of have an idea of what the lyric might be at a certain point. But it’s actually — it’s not an ideal way to make a record with anybody, if you’re really © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-

making music in the human way. You know music is made very differently now for the most part. You extract a rhythm track from Marvin Gaye, as we know from hearing about the Pharrell — Robin Thicke stuff and they extract this idea from that one, and often times they are fragments of files, sound files, that are actually lifted. I can’t tell you how many times I’ve heard a James Brown drum part, or even James Brown making a sound inserted into somebody’s song. And the result is like yeah, some of it feels great and…
